quiz.question: A caller says they're from your bank's 'security team' and asks you to move your savings to a 'safe account' immediately. What's the safest response?
options: Ask for a confirmation SMS, then do as they say
Hang up and call your bank on its official number
Give them your card PIN so they can verify you
Move the money quickly to be safe
quiz.explanation: Banks don't ask customers to transfer money to 'safe accounts'. Caller IDs and SMS senders can be spoofed, so confirm through a channel you control.

quiz.question: Why do scammers prefer payments in crypto or gift cards?
options: They're hard to trace and to reverse
They're cheaper for the person paying
They're more strictly regulated
Banks require them for investments
quiz.explanation: Card payments and bank transfers sometimes leave room for recovery; crypto and gift cards rarely do.

quiz.question: True or false: a genuine investment opportunity will rarely require you to decide within hours.
options: False, unless you pay a reservation fee
False, good deals always vanish in minutes
True, but only for crypto opportunities
True — real offers give you time to check
quiz.explanation: Real offers may have deadlines, but they're documented and give you reasonable time. Extreme urgency is designed to stop you thinking.

quiz.question: An 'adviser' you've never met has called three times this week, praising your intelligence and saying 'smart people like you act fast'. Which tactic is this?
options: A sign of a high-quality product
Helpful diversification advice
Flattery plus urgency to rush you
Standard, regulated investment advice
quiz.explanation: Repeated unsolicited calls, flattery and time pressure are textbook manipulation. Check whether the firm is authorised before engaging.

units.title: Startups & venture capital
units.description: How startups raise money, how ownership gets diluted, and how venture funds make returns.

levels.name: How startups raise money
levels.subtitle: From seed to Series A and beyond

cards.title: Funding stages
cards.body: Startups often raise money in stages: pre-seed and seed (idea, first product), Series A (proving the business model), then Series B, C… to scale.

cards.title: Who invests
cards.body: Early money often comes from founders, friends, business angels and seed funds. Venture capital funds usually join as the company grows.

cards.title: Equity, not loans
cards.body: Investors usually receive shares, not loans. They make money only if the company becomes more valuable and there's an exit, such as a sale or a stock-market listing.

quiz.question: At which stage is a startup typically still testing whether customers really want its product?
options: Series B
Series C
Stock-market listing (IPO)
Pre-seed / seed
quiz.explanation: Early rounds fund the search for product–market fit. Later rounds typically fund scaling a model that already works.

quiz.question: How do early startup investors usually get their money back?
options: Through monthly interest payments on their money
Through an exit: a sale or a stock-market listing
Through dividends paid from the first year
The company must repay them after five years
quiz.explanation: Startups rarely pay dividends; they reinvest everything in growth. Without an exit, investors' shares are hard to sell.

quiz.question: True or false: a startup that has raised a very large round is sure to succeed.
options: True, if top VC funds took part
False — many well-funded startups fail
True, investors only fund likely winners
False, but only in hardware startups
quiz.explanation: Lots of money can delay failure, but it doesn't fix a missing market or a broken business model.

quiz.question: What is a business angel?
options: An individual investing their own money early
A government agency that gives grants
A bank that specialises in startup loans
A fund that only buys listed shares
quiz.explanation: Angels often invest before VC funds, sometimes bringing advice and contacts as well as money.

quiz.question: Which statement is FALSE?
options: Investors often get special rights attached to their shares
Each funding round usually sets a new valuation
Startup shares can usually be sold easily at any time, like listed shares
Startup shares are illiquid until an exit
quiz.explanation: There's no daily market for private company shares; selling before an exit is often difficult or restricted.

cards.title: Two valuations
cards.body: Pre-money valuation is the company's value before new money comes in. Post-money = pre-money + the new investment.

cards.title: Who owns what
cards.body: The new investor's stake = investment ÷ post-money valuation. For example, 1M CHF into a 4M pre-money gives 1M ÷ 5M = 20%.

cards.title: A price, not a certainty
cards.body: A valuation is what investors agreed to pay at that moment. It can go up, or down in a later 'down round'.

quiz.question: A startup raises 1M CHF at a 4M CHF pre-money valuation. What stake does the new investor get?
quiz.explanation: Post-money = 4M + 1M = 5M, and 1M ÷ 5M = 20%. 25% wrongly divides by the pre-money valuation.

quiz.question: An investor pays 2M CHF for 10% of a startup. What are the post-money and pre-money valuations?
options: 20M CHF post-money, 18M CHF pre-money
2M CHF post-money, 0 CHF pre-money
10M CHF post-money, 8M CHF pre-money
20M CHF pre-money, 22M CHF post-money
quiz.explanation: 2M ÷ 10% = 20M post-money; subtracting the new 2M gives 18M pre-money.

quiz.question: What happens in a 'down round'?
options: The company is sold to a larger competitor
The number of shares is cut in half
Investors get their original money back
It raises money at a lower valuation than before
quiz.explanation: Down rounds signal that expectations have fallen, and they usually dilute existing shareholders more heavily.

quiz.question: True or false: a startup valued at 50M CHF has 50M CHF in the bank.
options: True, right after a funding round
False, it always has more than that
True, the valuation equals its cash
False — valuation isn't cash
quiz.explanation: A valuation reflects expectations about future value. The cash is only what investors actually put in, minus what's been spent.

quiz.question: Offer A invests 2M CHF at an 8M pre-money; offer B invests 2M CHF at a 6M pre-money. All else equal, which leaves the founders with more ownership?
options: Offer A — the investor gets 20% instead of 25%
Offer B, because lower valuations favour founders
Both — 2M is 2M
Impossible to compare
quiz.explanation: A: 2 ÷ 10 = 20%; B: 2 ÷ 8 = 25%. In practice, other terms in the deal matter too.

levels.name: Dilution
levels.subtitle: Smaller slices of a bigger cake

cards.title: What is dilution?
cards.body: When a company issues new shares, existing shareholders own a smaller percentage. Their stake can still be worth more if the valuation grows.

cards.title: Round after round
cards.body: Dilution compounds: a founder with 60% who gives up 20% in a round keeps 60% × 0.8 = 48%.

cards.title: Option pools
cards.body: Startups often reserve shares for future employees (an option pool), which also dilutes existing holders.

quiz.question: A founder owns 60%. A new round issues shares equal to 20% of the company afterwards. What does the founder own now?
quiz.explanation: 60% × (1 − 0.20) = 48%. 40% wrongly subtracts 20 percentage points instead of 20% of the stake.

quiz.question: A founder owns 50%. The seed round dilutes everyone by 20%, then Series A by 15%. What does the founder own after both?
quiz.explanation: 50% × 0.80 × 0.85 = 34%. 15% subtracts the percentages directly, which is how dilution does NOT work.

quiz.question: True or false: dilution always makes a founder poorer.
options: True, unless there's no new round
False — the slice can be worth more
True, a smaller percentage means less money
False, dilution only affects the investors
quiz.explanation: 50% of a 2M company is 1M; 40% of a 10M company is 4M. What matters is the value of the slice.

quiz.question: Why do startups create an employee option pool?
options: To attract staff with a stake in success
To pay back early investors over time
To lower the founders' tax bill
To protect founders from any dilution
quiz.explanation: Options let early-stage companies compete for talent despite paying lower salaries — at the cost of some dilution.

quiz.question: Which statement is FALSE?
options: Once you own 10% of a startup, that percentage is fixed forever
Some investors negotiate the right to keep their stake by investing again
Dilution can be worth it if the new money creates enough value
New rounds usually dilute existing shareholders
quiz.explanation: Percentages change with every new share issue; 'pro-rata' rights let some investors buy in again to keep their share.

cards.title: Most don't make it
cards.body: Most startups fail or return little to their investors. Building a new business under uncertainty is hard, even with a strong team.

cards.title: Common reasons
cards.body: Frequent causes include no real market need, running out of cash, competition, a weak business model and team problems.

cards.title: Survivorship bias
cards.body: We hear about famous successes, not the thousands that quietly closed. That makes startup success look far more common than it is.

quiz.question: Which is among the most frequently cited reasons startups fail?
options: They didn't have a patent
The founders were too young
They launched before the product was perfect
There wasn't enough real demand for the product
quiz.explanation: Building something people don't need is a classic failure. Launching early and imperfect is often a deliberate strategy to learn faster.

quiz.question: A startup has 600'000 CHF in the bank and spends 50'000 CHF more each month than it earns. What is its 'runway'?
options: 12 months
50 months
Unlimited, as long as it has customers
6 months
quiz.explanation: 600'000 ÷ 50'000 = 12 months before the cash runs out, unless it cuts costs, grows revenue or raises more money.

quiz.question: True or false: some famous founders dropped out of university and succeeded, so dropping out increases your chance of success.
options: True, these famous examples prove it
False — that's survivorship bias
False, because a degree guarantees success
True, but only for tech startups
quiz.explanation: Looking only at winners hides the base rate. A few memorable stories don't show what's typical.

quiz.question: A startup is growing users fast but loses money on every customer. Why can this be dangerous?
options: Investors require startups to lose money
Losses always turn into profits at scale
Faster growth can mean faster cash burn
It's never a problem while users are growing
quiz.explanation: If each customer costs more than they bring in, scale magnifies losses. Growth only helps once 'unit economics' work.

quiz.question: Which statement is FALSE?
options: Running out of cash is a common cause of failure
A startup with a strong team cannot fail
Many startups change their product along the way (a 'pivot')
Timing can matter a lot for a startup's success
quiz.explanation: A strong team improves the odds but can't remove market, timing and funding risks.

cards.title: The power law
cards.body: VC returns are highly concentrated: a few big winners usually make up most of a fund's gains, while many investments return little or nothing.

cards.title: The fund model
cards.body: Investors (limited partners) commit money to a fund for about 10 years. The managers (general partners) usually charge a yearly management fee plus a share of profits, often around 20% ('carried interest').

cards.title: Why VCs swing big
cards.body: Because most bets fail, each investment needs the potential to return the whole fund. Modest successes can't make up for many losses.

quiz.question: A fund invests 1M CHF in each of 10 startups. Seven return nothing, two return 1M CHF each, and one returns 30M CHF. What multiple of its money does the fund make before fees?
quiz.explanation: (0 + 2 + 30) ÷ 10 = 3.2× — despite 7 failures out of 10. 3.0× counts only the big winner and forgets the two 1M returns.

quiz.question: In that same fund, roughly what share of all the money returned came from the single winner?
options: About 94%
About 30%
About 50%
About 10%
quiz.explanation: 30M of the 32M returned ≈ 94%. That's the power law: one outlier drives almost the whole result.

quiz.question: True or false: a VC fund with 7 failures out of 10 investments must be a bad fund.
options: True, a good fund avoids most failures
True, unless the failed bets were cheap
False — one big winner can carry the fund
False, failures simply don't count in VC
quiz.explanation: Failure rates alone say little. What matters is whether the winners are big enough to cover the losses many times over.

quiz.question: Why do VCs often look for startups that could become very large, rather than solid small businesses?
options: Because large companies never fail
Because a few huge winners must cover the many losses
Because small businesses can't legally raise money
Because VCs are paid per company
quiz.explanation: A solid business that returns 2× can't offset several zeros. VCs need outliers that can return the whole fund.

quiz.question: What is 'carried interest' in a VC fund?
options: Interest charged on loans to startups
The managers' share of profits, often ~20%
A yearly fee on the money committed
Interest earned on the fund's spare cash
quiz.explanation: The yearly fee is the management fee; carried interest is paid only out of profits, aligning managers with investors.
